# Hard-to-vary report: Bostrom, "Are You Living in a Computer Simulation?"

## 1. The question, frozen

The title asks whether *you* are in a simulation. But the abstract and conclusion make a narrower claim central, and I test that one: **at least one of (1) almost all human-level civilizations go extinct before "posthuman," (2) almost no posthuman civilization runs many ancestor-simulations, (3) almost all minds like ours are simulated — is true.** Range: any civilization that could reach posthuman technological capacity. This is not one of the six ordinary kinds of question the method lists; it is a **derived disjunction** (an "if the premises hold, one of three must" proof-step) wrapped in an **argument** whose premises are empirical/philosophical. That mix decides which tests apply below: the derivation itself is tested by removing a condition and finding a counter-case, not by "flip," per the method's own carve-out for derived conclusions. Fixed by the author, stated openly: the paper does not claim to say *which* disjunct is true (he only later guesses "roughly even" credence).

## 2. The explanation in parts

- **P1 Substrate-independence:** a computer running the right program would be conscious, at least at fine (synaptic-level) simulation.
- **P2 Computing-power estimates:** posthuman civilizations could cheaply run huge numbers of ancestor-simulations (~10^33–10^36 ops per simulation vs. ~10^42 ops/sec available).
- **P3 The identity:** f_sim = f_P·f_I·N_I / (f_P·f_I·N_I + 1) — a bookkeeping equation from the definitions of the four quantities.
- **P4 Bland indifference principle:** with no information telling you apart from the rest of the reference class, your credence should equal the class's fraction.
- **P5 "No distinguishing information" clause:** the (unstated-as-a-test) assumption that we currently have no evidence bearing on whether our own experience is simulated.

## 3. Part by part

| Part | Mark | Why |
|---|---|---|
| P1 Substrate-independence | **Held if** | Only P1 keeps disjunct (3) alive as a live option; drop it and there's no route to simulated minds at all, so the trilemma collapses to "we're certainly biological." The author himself flags it as "not entirely uncontroversial" — asserted, not built here. |
| P2 Computing-power estimates | **Held** | Swapped for wildly different figures (author explicitly tries several orders of magnitude off) and N_I stays "extremely large." Built from independent, cross-checked physical estimates (Drexler, Bradbury, Lloyd, Moravec), not just one fitted number. |
| P3 The identity | **Held** | It is arithmetic given the definitions; nothing to swap. Built, not asserted. |
| "N_I extremely large" (inside P2/P3) | **Held** | Remove it (suppose posthuman civilizations run on average only one or two ancestor-simulations) and the trilemma stops being forced — moderate f_P, f_I, f_sim all become consistent. This is the part that gives the argument its bite. |
| P4 Bland indifference principle | **Held**, against the nearest rival | Swapped for the stronger Self-Sampling Assumption behind the Doomsday argument, the paper names the difference (SSA needs random sampling across *time*; P4 only needs no info distinguishing you *within* a class at one time) and defends P4 as the weaker, more defensible claim — a real rival was built and told apart, not just waved off. |
| P5 "No distinguishing information" | **Unknown / catch-all with no gauge** | The clause can always be invoked ("we have no such information") or always denied ("of course we do — I feel too normal to be simulated") with no stated test for which is so. No gauge is given for when this catch-all is or isn't swallowing the job. |
| Substrate-independence × P5 interaction | **Pull, unaddressed** | If minds can be simulated (P1) and simulations are common (conclusion of (3)), a careful simulated observer might expect some detectable trace (a "glitch") — which would itself be distinguishing information and disable P4. The paper doesn't test this pull; it simply asserts "the implications are not that radical." |

## 4. Whole-explanation checks

- **Flip:** not the right test here — the trilemma is a derived conclusion, not a story fit to one outcome. The proof-style test (remove a condition, find a counter-case) is the one that bites, and it locates the real load: "N_I extremely large," not the specific numbers.
- **Hunt for the answer in the starting points:** no circularity found — f_P, f_I, N_I, H are defined independently of the conclusion, and the surprising work is done by an empirical claim (astronomical computing power), not by a hidden restatement of the conclusion.
- **Rivals:** the paper itself builds and dismisses the nearest rival (the Doomsday argument's SSA) by naming a real difference. That is good practice, done in the text.
- **Where the jobs came from:** the job "must survive any timescale to posthumanity" and "must survive being off by orders of magnitude" are both given by the author explicitly and both pass — genuine stress-tests, not ones I supplied.
- **Catch-alls and gauges:** P5 is a catch-all with no gauge (see above). "Ancestor-simulation" itself is loosely bounded, but the author flags this openly (me-simulations, shadow-people) rather than hiding it, so it counts as an honestly-marked limit, not a silent one.
- **What the change list leaves out:** the paper never runs the test "suppose a simulated observer could detect the simulation" — a change that could matter and is not on the list, not flagged as excluded either.
- **Borrowed:** substrate-independence borrows from philosophy-of-mind functionalism debates not settled here; the full defense of the indifference principle is borrowed from the author's other work (cited, not repeated).

## 5. What would make it harder to vary

The two best moves: (a) give P5 a gauge — state what evidence, if we had it, *would* count as telling us we're atypical, so the indifference step isn't a free pass either way; (b) address the P1×P5 pull directly — either argue that a good simulation is in principle undetectable from inside (closing the gap) or concede that (3) being true would itself generate exactly the distinguishing information P4 requires absence of.

## 6. What this does not show

Passing these tests shows the trilemma's derivation is tight and its main premises (computing power, the indifference principle against its nearest rival) are held, not that any one of (1), (2), (3) is actually true, and not that you are or are not in a simulation.

## 7. One next step

Ask: what observation, in principle, would count as the "distinguishing information" whose absence P4 requires — and check whether the paper's own claim that we might detect our simulation being visibly edited or rerun (Section III) already counts as exactly that kind of evidence.
